title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money, Death, and the Thames

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
Our Mutual Friend is, in many ways, his most ambitious and most unsettling book.
It opens with a corpse fished from the Thames, and it never quite lets you forget that image.
Money, death, identity, and the river — these are the novel's great obsessions, and they are ours for this series.
I'm joined today by three remarkable readers, each of whom brings a quite different lens to this book.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don — a critic in the great tradition who reads novels as moral investigations of character.
He is, I should warn you, occasionally withering — but always with exquisite courtesy.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who has spent a career mapping the real institutions behind the fictional ones.
He knows what it actually meant to be poor in Victorian London — and he does not let us forget it.
And Oliver Trevelyan has read more classic novels aloud than perhaps anyone alive.
He is an actor and writer who hears the rhythm of a sentence the way a musician hears a phrase — and he is very good company.
Today we begin at the beginning — with the novel's great themes of money, death, and what the Thames means when Dickens looks into it.
What strikes me, every time I return to this novel, is how quickly Dickens puts death on the table.
Not as melodrama — as arithmetic.
A body in the river is, from the very first pages, simultaneously a tragedy and a financial instrument.
And then Dickens gives us the Boffins — this gloriously warm, hopelessly unfashionable couple — and the tonal shift is almost violent.
You go from the river and its dead to a sitting room full of goodwill and domesticity.
That contrast is absolutely deliberate, and it is one of the things that makes this novel so endlessly readable.
Oliver is right to flag the Boffins as a tonal corrective — but I'd press a little further on what Dickens is doing there morally.
The passage is at once tender and quietly devastating in its irony.
Mr Boffin looks at his wife and says, with complete sincerity:
'Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!'
And Dickens's narrating voice responds — with what I can only describe as affectionate ruthlessness — that this was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations.
They sit together, and Dickens pronounces them — the word is exact — a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
The capitalisation of Unfashionable is Dickens at his most pointed — virtue and vulgarity, in his world, are sentenced together.
What Edmund describes as irony has, from where I stand, a rather specific social content.
The Boffins are new money — dust-heap money — and fashionability is the particular currency of aspiration in a society whose class markers are constantly shifting.
Dickens understands, with great precision, that goodness and social fluency are not the same thing — and in this world, they may be mutually exclusive.
But I want to draw us also to a passage that strikes me as equally central to the novel's opening atmosphere — the train crossing the Thames.
Dickens writes the railway with extraordinary controlled violence.

'The train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare.'
That word — bomb-shell — is not decorative.
Industry and modernity arrive in this novel with the force of an explosion — tearing down, crossing over, spending themselves in smoke.
And Dickens keeps going — which is the thing that always astonishes me on a second reading.
He gives you the bomb-shell, the explosion — and then immediately pulls the camera back to Father Time.
The train goes straight to its end, he writes, 'as Father Time goes to his.'
'To whom it is no matter what living waters run high or low, reflect the heavenly lights and darknesses, produce their little growth of weeds and flowers.'
In the space of one paragraph, you've gone from a Victorian railway timetable to a meditation on eternity.
That's not a novelist showing off — that's a novelist who has completely dissolved the boundary between the immediate and the cosmic.
And it is precisely that dissolution — if I may borrow Oliver's term — that prepares the reader for Bradley Headstone.
If the Boffins represent what goodness costs in social terms, Bradley Headstone represents what the suppression of passion costs in human ones.
There is a description of him, sitting through an entire night, that I find among the most genuinely frightening things in the novel.

'Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.'
Charmed flame — turning him old.
The fire does not warm him; it consumes him from inside, ageing him in the space of a single night.
Dickens understood — in a way that I think is still underestimated — that guilt and repression are physical processes, not merely psychological ones.
Edmund's reading of Headstone is compelling — though I'd add that Bradley is also, quite specifically, a man of a new social class.
He is the educated poor — the schoolteacher who has violently dragged himself up through self-improvement — and the violence is literally written on his body by the time we see him in that passage.
The respectable surface degenerating — the hair, the face — is also the surface of an entire class ideology falling apart.
Dickens does not sentimentalise the aspiring poor here — he gives them their full tragic weight.
Three passages, and already we have the full architecture of the novel — warmth and irony, modernity and eternity, aspiration and destruction.
In our next segment, we'll go deeper into the river itself — what it carries, what it conceals, and what Dickens makes it mean.

segments.title: The Dust Heaps: Wealth from Refuse

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel and opens it up, layer by layer.
Our Mutual Friend is a book about money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and how a society organises itself around its pursuit.
And the central image Dickens chose for all of that is, magnificently, a heap of dust.
Today we are exploring that image and the social world it generates — the beggars, the nouveaux riches, the dispossessed, and the desperately pretending.
With me are three readers I trust absolutely with this material.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings the moral and literary intelligence of a lifetime with the English novel — he will keep us honest about what Dickens is actually doing as a storyteller.
Professor James Blackstone arrives with the historical and legal scaffolding — he knows what poverty actually meant in mid-Victorian England, and he will not let us forget it.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, narrator of more classic novels than any man living — hears the music in this prose the way a conductor hears a score.
Let us begin with the novel's social architecture — specifically, a man named Twemlow and his peculiar function in the Veneering household.
The Veneerings are the novel's great emblem of new money — everything in their house, including their guests, is brand new and surfaces all the way down.
And Twemlow is their most useful social acquisition — not because of anything he says or does, but because of who his cousin happens to be.
Dickens renders this with a metaphor so precise it amounts to a sociological theorem.
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
He is furniture — useful, portable, kept in a livery stable-yard when not required.
And the cruelest touch is the structural logic: the more guests are added, the further Twemlow is pushed from the centre of the table.
Social prestige works exactly like that — you are only as central as you are scarce.
What strikes me about Twemlow is that Dickens gives him an inner life the metaphor almost obscures.
He is described as a source of "blind confusion" to the Veneerings — he cannot quite comprehend what is being done to him.
That is not satire of Twemlow — that is satire of a world so thoroughly mercenary that a decent man genuinely cannot read it.
Dickens is always more interested in the moral texture of bewilderment than in the mechanics of exploitation.
And the comedy of it — the physical comedy — is that the man has been stored over a livery stable in Duke Street.
Not a flat, not a club — a livery stable-yard.
He is on easy castors, wheeled out when needed and wheeled back when not.
You can hear Dickens timing that gag — the revelation of "easy castors" arrives just after you have been asked to take the dinner-table metaphor perfectly seriously.
He builds the absurdity one degree at a time, and then, precisely when you think it cannot go further, he pulls Twemlow out to his utmost extent of twenty leaves.
That sense of mechanical extension is everywhere in the novel's treatment of new wealth — things and people stretched beyond their natural limits.
James, when we turn from the glittering Veneering table to the Boffin household, the register changes entirely — and one passage in particular stands out for its raw feeling.
The Boffins arrived at their wealth through the dust heaps — they are, in the Victorian sense, people of the yard rather than the drawing room.

And what makes this passage so important is that it shows us what that world produced — not just wealth, but a kind of rough, genuine human tenderness that the Veneerings could not have manufactured on any budget.
Boffin is recounting the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon — a child of seven, being sent alone to a foreign school by a father who would not spare sixpence for a coach.
The passage that follows is, I think, one of the most genuinely moving things in the novel.
"There was his little scanty travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the steamboat."
"Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks."

"But seeing the tears come into the child's eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, 'I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!'"
The repetition — "wide wide world" — is not a slip; it is grief speaking, the way grief actually repeats itself.
This is precisely where Dickens locates his moral authority in this novel — not in the educated classes, not in the institutions, but in a woman kneeling at a yard fire.
Burke would have recognised something here — the affections, the small domestic bonds, as the foundation of any social order worth the name.
And there is a detail that undoes me every time — "he rests his heart against her bosom, and looks up at both of us, as if it was in pain — in agony."
That child is, structurally, the dead man around whose estate the entire novel turns — and yet we know him first as a look of agony remembered across decades.
When I recorded this passage I had to take a long pause before "wide wide world" — not a theatrical pause, a genuine one.
Because Boffin is a man speaking in dialect, with imperfect grammar, and Dickens trusts him completely with the most important emotional material in this section of the book.
"I went aboard with him — I gave him first what little treat I thought he'd like" — seven words buried in the middle of the speech, and they break your heart quietly.
That is the genius of it — the tenderness is enacted in the doing, not announced.
And this same fortune that inspired such tenderness in the Boffins — once word of it gets out — attracts a very different kind of humanity altogether.
The Secretary in the novel becomes a kind of archivist of desperation — and Dickens's taxonomy of beggars is one of the great comic passages in his work.
The catalogue of beggars is one of those passages where Dickens is showing off — and he knows he's showing off — and it is spectacular.
There are daughters of general officers — "long accustomed to every luxury of life," Dickens says, and then cannot resist — "except spelling."
Two words. The parenthesis does the whole satirical work in two words.
But the line I love best is his description of their documents.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
Minced veal to a calf — the distance between the real thing and the fraudulent representation of it, collapsed into one absurd culinary image.
What makes this more than comic is the accuracy — these categories of letter-writing beggar were entirely real and entirely familiar to Dickens's contemporary readers.
The wives writing without their husbands' knowledge, the husbands writing without their wives' — it is a portrait of private financial shame that crossed every class.
And then there are the punctual business-habits beggars — those who set a precise deadline for their own death if no money arrives.
The comedy is black enough to make you stop laughing midway through it.
I find myself resistant to reading this purely as social satire, even here.
What Dickens is also doing — and what I think matters more — is showing us the moral disfigurement that poverty enacts on the people it catches.
These beggars are not simply victims of an unjust system — they are people who have had their honesty and dignity corroded by necessity.
That is the deeper cruelty Dickens is pointing at — and Oliver's delight in the catalogue risks, only slightly, letting us off the hook.
Sir Edmund is entirely right — and I take the rebuke in the spirit it was intended, which is to say, graciously and with mild indignation.
But I would say that Dickens himself is laughing — he is not coldly anatomizing from a distance.
The laughter and the pity are not in sequence — they are simultaneous.
And wealth, in this novel, attracts not only beggars from outside, but predators from within.
Silas Wegg — one of Dickens's great comic villains — believes he has found a will that will allow him to blackmail Boffin out of his entire fortune.
Wegg reading aloud a will he has just discovered — and which he believes to be devastating — is one of the great comic performances Dickens writes for a single character.
He is "blandly and buoyantly" delivering what he imagines to be a death blow.
The will itself is wonderfully terse — Dickens gives us the entire moral history of old Harmon in two clauses.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
"Quite enough for him" — three words that carry a lifetime of contempt from father to servant.
The legal language — "rest and residue" — functions here as a kind of final insult: cold, formulaic, and total.
The Crown gets everything because there is no one the old man wished to benefit — that is a portrait of a man hollowed out by misanthropy.
And the irony Wegg cannot see — that he is reading an instrument that diminishes both Boffin and the object of Wegg's own greed — is exquisitely managed.
From a legal standpoint, the fact that this will could supersede the one leaving the fortune to Boffin — and that the Crown stood as residual legatee — was not fantastic invention.
Intestacy law and competing wills were a genuine source of social chaos in mid-Victorian England, and the Courts of Chancery made fortunes for lawyers while destroying them for everyone else.
Dickens knew this territory from the inside — and Wegg's scene has a documentary accuracy beneath its farce.
From the farce of Wegg to something altogether darker — one of the most unsettling confrontations in the novel.
Riderhood has been watching Bradley Headstone very carefully — and what he has seen gives him a power he intends to use with absolute ruthlessness.
Riderhood is the novel's great exemplar of the lowest-rung predator — a man with nothing but information, deploying it with the precision of a professional extortionist.
The speech he delivers to Bradley Headstone is a masterclass in blackmail — every sentence is a further demonstration of how much he knows.
"I've got your Bargeman's clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the blows."
"I've got them, and I've got you."
Five words — and they are the most efficient sentence of coercion in the novel.
The rhythm of Riderhood's speech is hypnotic — it has the structure of an incantation: "I see you," "I know you," "I've got you."
And then the repetition at the end — "I'll be paid for it — I'll be paid for it — I'll be paid for it" — three times, like a curse being sealed.
Dickens understands that obsession repeats — that the compulsive mind circles back to its fixation with a kind of terrible music.
And yet what makes this scene morally complex is that Bradley Headstone is himself a murderer.
Riderhood's evil here is not greater than the evil it feeds upon — the two men are locked in a moral descent that neither can arrest.
The phrase "till I've drained you dry" — that is the language of the parasite, certainly, but also of a man describing what the whole money-system of the novel does to everyone within it.
The dust heap generates wealth, the wealth generates predation — and the predators find their own predators in turn.
And before we close this segment, there is one more passage that brings us back to the surface of that world — not to its violence or its grief, but to its comedy of appearance.
Oliver — Sloppy's new suit.
Sloppy's new suit is a scene I could read every day for the rest of my life and still find fresh.
Mrs Boffin has had him dressed in his best — the tailor has been specifically instructed to conceal the buttons.
And then Dickens delivers the verdict.
"He now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
A perfect Argus in the way of buttons — it is the single best use of classical mythology for comedic purposes in the English language.
And then: the hat, the sleeves, the trousers, the "yawning gulf at his waistband" — Sloppy's body is simply too alive, too much itself, for any suit ever made.
There is something genuine underneath the comedy — Sloppy is being dressed up to enter a social world that does not quite fit him in any sense.
The buttons cannot be hidden because his body will not submit to the concealment — it is a small, comic version of what the novel does to every character who tries to disguise what they are.
Sloppy's buttons refuse to be concealed in exactly the way Riderhood's knowledge refuses to be contained — both are eruptions of the real into the constructed surface.
The novel trusts the comedy to carry that weight — and it does.
Wealth from refuse, dignity from buttons, tenderness from a yard in the shadow of a dust heap — this novel holds all of it at once.
My thanks to Sir Edmund Leigh, Professor James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan for a conversation that has done justice to Dickens's extraordinary range in this segment.
We will continue unpacking Our Mutual Friend in our next segment — do stay with us.

segments.title: Bella's Desire: The Golden Dustman's Daughter

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, chapter by chapter, to see what makes it tick.

Today we're deep inside the world of Bella Wilfer — the golden dustman's daughter, the girl left a fortune by a man she never met, and the novel's most searching study of what money does to character.
With me today are three remarkable readers of this novel.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes great fiction is ultimately about individual moral character — goodness, weakness, self-sacrifice — and he reads Dickens with that unflinching conviction.
Professor James Blackstone brings the social historian's eye — the real institutions, the real poverty, the real law — that sit behind Dickens's invented world.
And Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice of more classic novels than any living person — hears the novel as it was always meant to be heard: performed, timed, relished.
The question before us today is this: what does Bella Wilfer want, and what does the novel ask her to give up in order to get it?
One ought to begin, I think, by insisting that Bella Wilfer is not simply a study in greed reformed.
That is the reductive reading, and Dickens is too subtle a moralist to settle for it.
What she wants, at the novel's outset, is dignity — the dignity that money appears to guarantee in a society that has taught her, from childhood, that she is a commodity.
The old miser Harmon bequeathed her — bequeathed her, like a piece of furniture — to a son she had never met.
And John Harmon himself, lying in that public-house bed, recovering from the attempt on his life, understands the obscenity of it.
He tells us — and this passage has always struck me as the moral hinge of the entire novel —
"the thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella."
Proving Bella — not testing her vanity, but genuinely trying to discover whether the person behind the money-hunger is someone capable of love and loyalty.
Edmund is right to put the word 'proving' at the centre, but I want to press on the mechanism behind it — because what Harmon is doing is, in institutional terms, astonishing.
He is, in effect, conducting a social experiment under false pretences, with a woman who has no knowledge she is being observed.
Now, the novel frames this as romantic and redemptive, and I do not entirely resist that framing.
But one must notice that the phrase Harmon uses — "the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches" — tells us something precise about how money works in this novel.
The Harmon fortune is dust — literally, dust from the rubbish heaps — and it corrupts everything it touches, unless the person who inherits it can prove themselves untouched.
The contrast with Bella's own background is worth dwelling on.
Lizzie Hexam describes a child Bella knows — a poor ailing little creature — and she says, with that terrible parenthesis:
"This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley."
That aside — 'if she ever had one' — is five words that contain an entire world of want.
James, that parenthesis is one of Dickens's signature moves — the sudden drop into the unspoken, the thing that lands like a stone.
When I read that passage aloud, I always take a breath before 'if she ever had one' — and then let the silence do the rest.
But I want to come at Bella from a slightly different angle — through Eugene Wrayburn, of all people.
Because the novel is full of characters who are pre-determined by their fathers — and Eugene's account of his own family is one of the funniest things in the entire book.
He describes his father — M. R. F., the Most Ridiculous Father — disposing of each child at birth, as casually as one might label a parcel.
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.' Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one — the timing of that is perfect, and the comedy is devastatingly serious.
Because Bella has been labelled by a father figure too — old Harmon — and the novel's great question is whether she can tear that label off.
Oliver, that parallel is shrewder than it might first appear.
The paternal disposition of children — as though they were estates to be managed — is everywhere in this novel.
And it is precisely the antithesis of what Dickens believes character ought to be: something earned, not inherited, not imposed.
Now, there is a counter-movement in the novel — and this is where I think the Wegg and Venus subplot earns its place — which is the naked exposure of what the alternative to virtue looks like.
Silas Wegg's scheme is a masterpiece of comic villainy, but it is also, morally speaking, deeply instructive.
Here is what Wegg proposes, in his magnificent circumlocutory style:
"he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!'"
And then Boffin, if he resists, is to be kept — and I find this phrase almost Miltonic in its portentousness —
"in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions."
The language of moral bondage applied to a scheme of pure extortion — that is Dickens at his most savagely ironic.
The legal historian in me cannot let that pass without noting that Wegg's scheme is, in structural terms, blackmail — a criminal offence that English law was still quite uncertain about in the 1860s.
But what Dickens does — and this is the genius of the Boffin subplot — is show us that the Harmon money attracts precisely this kind of predation.
The dust heaps breed vultures.
And the question the novel keeps asking — the question Harmon keeps asking about Bella — is whether the money will do the same thing to her.
And then Dickens answers that question in the most deliberately domestic, almost anti-climactic way imaginable — with a supper.
When Bella and John Rokesmith — and old R. Wilfer, bless him — finally sit down together in poverty and happiness, the narrator reaches for a fairy-tale image.
And it is, I think, one of the most quietly perfect passages in the novel.

"It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, 'Somebody's been drinking my milk!'"
"It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made."
The hobgoblins are absent — and with them, all the threatening thunder of old Harmon's wealth.
What remains is just people, eating, happy — and Dickens has the nerve to call it the most delicious meal any of them has ever had.
That is not sentimentality — that is a considered moral argument, delivered in the idiom of a fairy story.

Oliver is quite right, and I would add one thing: the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles — those brass knobs staring from the corner like the eyes of some dull dragon — is still there in the room.
Dickens does not pretend the world of money has been abolished — he shows it watching, reduced to a dull and powerless thing.
And against that, he places the terrible opposite extreme — Bradley Headstone, who has not Bella's capacity for transformation.
Headstone is a study in what happens when the moral will collapses entirely — not into greed, but into something darker.
The narrator tells us, with the precision of a diagnostician:
"He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently."
The absence of remorse is not relief — it is its own form of damnation.
Bella's transformation is only legible against a darkness like that — the novel needs Headstone to show us what the refusal of change costs.

That psychological portrait of Headstone is extraordinary because it is, in effect, a description of compulsive repetition — what we might now recognise as a symptom of severe trauma — rendered in the language of moral theology.
Dickens is writing, in 1865, about something psychiatry would not properly name for another century.
But what I find remarkable is how it circles back to the novel's central argument about Bella.
Headstone cannot change because he will not feel.
Bella changes because, when tested, she discovers that she can — and that the wanting of money was never really the deepest thing in her.
We've moved, in the course of this conversation, from a man labelling his sons at birth, to a woman proving herself by choosing poverty, to a murderer trapped in the eternal repetition of his crime.
What this novel understands — and what our guests have illuminated so well — is that character is not given; it is chosen, or it is refused.
We'll be back shortly to turn our attention to the river — and to what Dickens sees when he looks into its depths.

segments.title: The Comedy of Ambition and Manners

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart, passage by passage, to see how it works.
I'm your host, and today we're looking at one of the novel's great pleasures: the comedy of ambition and manners.
The way Dickens skewers social climbing, self-delusion, and the extraordinary lengths people will go to in the presence of new money.
With me today are three guests who bring very different lenses to this material.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and one of the great defenders of character-based reading — the view that the novel's moral imagination matters more than its social programme.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian who will tell us what the institutions Dickens depicts actually were, and what they cost real people.
And Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels than almost anyone alive, and who hears in Dickens's prose things the rest of us can barely read on the page.
Let's begin with the passage where Dickens gives us a masterclass in satirising charity — or rather, the performance of charity.
What strikes me first about this passage is its extraordinary syntactic energy.
The list of churches, parsonages, organs, and children accumulates with a kind of gleeful indignation — fifty-seven, forty-two, seven-and-twenty — the precision is the joke.
But the crowning moment — the one that reveals exactly what Dickens thinks of these arrangements — is the Duke of Linseed's letter.
'Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.'
Six words of physical description, and the entire world of aristocratic condescension is anatomised.
The letter is 'large' and 'fat' and 'private' — and yet it was, Dickens tells us, lithographed by the hundred.
That gap between the claim of intimacy and the reality of mass production is, to my mind, the moral centre of the passage.
Sir Edmund is right about the moral centre, though I'd want to add the institutional texture that makes the joke so precise.
The Stewardship system was entirely real, and thoroughly disreputable.
Charities in the mid-Victorian period routinely sold nominal positions — Steward, Patron, Vice-President — as a mechanism for extracting donations from the newly wealthy.
The fee granted the donor the temporary illusion of standing alongside actual aristocrats at a public dinner.
Dickens captures the postscript perfectly: 'The Steward's fee is limited to three Guineas.'
'Limited.' As though the Duke were protecting Boffin from his own generosity.
The whole apparatus of Victorian philanthropic theatre is in that one word.
I want to read that letter aloud one day with the Duke's full gravity — because the comic engine here runs entirely on voice.
Every sentence of that letter is a parody of a particular rhetorical register: the appeal to duty, the flattery of the recipient's distinction, the postscript that slides the fee in last.
And then the narrator's comment — 'Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript)' — is one of the driest lines in the whole novel.
What James has pointed out about the real institution makes it even better, because Dickens is not inventing absurdity — he is simply transcribing it.
And that is always the most devastating kind of satire.
From the satire of institutions, let's turn to the satire of self — and one of the novel's great comic voices.
Eugene Wrayburn is, among other things, a man who has made an art form of not knowing what he wants — and Oliver, this is very much your territory.
Eugene Wrayburn is one of the great performances in the novel — and I mean that very precisely.
He is performing boredom and self-ignorance with extraordinary artistry, and Dickens gives him the best lines to do it with.
Listen to how he explains himself to Mortimer.

'You know how dreadfully susceptible I am to boredom. You know that when I became enough of a man to find myself an embodied conundrum, I bored myself to the last degree by trying to find out what I meant.'
'An embodied conundrum.' That phrase is doing so much work.
It is a joke, and it is also a genuine description of a kind of modern identity crisis dressed up in the clothes of Regency langour.
And then: 'No. Upon my life, I can't.' The nursery riddle format deployed in response to the deepest question about the self.
I would gently resist the reading of Eugene as a species of modern alienation in fancy dress.
What we are seeing is a specific moral condition — the will that has never been tested, and therefore has never had occasion to discover itself.
Burke would have recognised it immediately: the man formed entirely by comfort, who mistakes inaction for a philosophical position.
The comedy is real and splendid.
But Dickens is also building the conditions for Eugene's later trial — and for his redemption, which only becomes possible because the conundrum eventually has an answer forced upon it.
What I find interesting here is the social position Eugene occupies.
He is a barrister, nominally, but he practises nothing and earns nothing.
He is the product of a system that trained gentlemen for the law as a form of social credentialing, not as a vocation.
So when he says he cannot discover what he means, he is also saying that the apparatus of his education and class has equipped him for nothing useful whatsoever.
The comic self-deprecation is entirely genuine, and entirely damning.
Now, the novel is also wonderfully funny about the institution of organised religion — not its spirit, but its administration.
Oliver, you have a passage about the Milveys and a parishioner named Mrs Sprodgkin that I think deserves some attention.
Mrs Sprodgkin is one of those minor characters Dickens creates in three strokes who then haunt you for the rest of your life.
She has a 'sixth sense' for detecting when the Milveys least want to see her, and arriving on the doorstep at precisely that moment.
The Milveys try to buy her off with tea, sugar, bread, and butter — and she accepts the gifts, and stays anyway.
And then she delivers what I can only describe as a masterpiece of sacred ingratitude.
'She regarded tea and sugar in the light of myrrh and frankincense, and considered bread and butter identical with locusts and wild honey.'
The biblical register elevated to receive a cup of tea and a loaf.
I defy anyone to read that sentence without hearing it as a completely straight delivery — which is of course what makes it irresistible.
What I admire in this passage is not merely the comedy, but the balance that follows it.
The narrator's final observation is, I think, entirely sincere: these are 'good Christian' people who 'merge the smallness of their work in its greatness.'
Dickens mocks the exacting parishioner, but he does not mock the vocation.
That distinction is very important to him throughout the novel, and it is one that critics who read him purely as a social reformer tend to miss.
The phrase 'incomprehensible humbugs' at the end of that passage is doing real work too.
It is not a condemnation of Mrs Sprodgkin — it is an acknowledgment that pastoral care in the Victorian parish routinely involved managing people who were, in any secular assessment, impossible.
The Milveys are representative of hundreds of real curates and their wives in small livings across England.
Dickens is honouring them — with comic precision, but genuinely honouring them.
Let's turn now to two of the novel's great comic reveal scenes — because Dickens is, among everything else, a superb craftsman of dramatic surprise.
Oliver, you have both of these — the scene with Bella and Mr Boffin, and the unmasking of Sloppy.
The Bella and Boffin scene is one of the tenderest moments in the novel — and it is also, in its own way, a comic scene, because Bella plays it as comedy.
She deposits the baby in John's arms — the Inexhaustible, as Dickens calls the child — and then kneels beside Boffin and launches into this magnificent cascade.
Listen to the rhythm of it.
'Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!'
Three 'please's in rapid succession — it is a child's grammar deployed to deliver an adult's epiphany.
And 'an exultant ringing laugh' is the stage direction.
Dickens knows this is a theatrical moment — he writes it for the stage even on the page.
What I find compelling about this scene is the moral reversal it enacts.
Bella has spent much of the novel defined by her worship of money — she confesses it openly, almost defiantly.
What the Boffin stratagem achieves — and it is an extraordinary piece of plotting — is to put her in the position of discovering that she values goodness more than she values wealth.
Not told so, not reasoned into it — but shown it, through the deliberate performance of its opposite.
And then, at the other end of the tonal register entirely — Sloppy.
The scene where Wegg's persecutor is unmasked is a pure piece of theatrical machinery — and it is perfection.
The entire set-up is in one sentence.
'Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.'
'Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.'
The sentence structure performs the revelation — you get 'a head that was whole' before you get 'a face that was Sloppy's,' so the surprise arrives in two beats.
Dickens knows exactly how to pace a reveal even at the level of the individual clause.
The 'fantail hat and velveteen smalls' deserve a word — this is working-class costume, very specifically.
The fantail hat was associated with dustmen and certain trades — it was a recognisable signifier of a particular social rank.
So the disguise works because it is a class disguise as much as a physical one.
And the humour of the reveal is partly that Sloppy — this gentle, simple, wonderful character — has been playing Wegg's sinister tormentor all along.
It is deeply satisfying — and, like so much in this novel, funnier for being absolutely just.
What I keep returning to, listening to all of you, is how capacious this novel's comedy is.
It can hold the Duke of Linseed's lithographed condescension, Mrs Sprodgkin's sacred ingratitude, Eugene's exquisite self-ignorance, and Sloppy's wonderful vindication — all in the same key.
In our next segment, we turn from comedy to something darker — the novel's sustained examination of what money does to those who pursue it.
Thank you all — Edmund, James, Oliver — for this.
Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We turn now to one of the novel's great structural puzzles: the hidden identity of John Harmon.
A man presumed dead, living under a false name in the very household of the people who inherited his fortune.
Dickens himself weighed in on what he was doing — and what he wasn't concealing.
Oliver Trevelyan has lived inside this novel's voices more than most — he'll open us in.
What Dickens does with Harmon is a sustained performance within a performance.
Rokesmith is the mask — but Harmon is also, in some ways, a mask.
And Dickens is beautifully candid about the game he was playing with his serial readership.
He tells us, in his own postscript note, exactly what the puzzle was designed to do.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
There's a teasing pleasure in that sentence — the writer winking at the audience while also defending his craft.
He trusted his readers, even as he tested them.
What strikes me in that passage is the phrase — 'in the interests of art.'
Dickens is making a claim for authorial sovereignty — that the artist, in his vocation, may be trusted to know what he is about.
That is not a modest claim. But it is not an immodest one either.
It is the assertion of a craftsman who has shaped his material deliberately.
And what gives the Harmon identity its moral weight is not the mystery itself, but what the disguise allows him to witness.
He sees the Boffins. He sees what they truly are.
And what he sees when he looks at the Boffins is a form of disinterestedness that the law simply could not enforce or even name.
Harmon, when he finally confronts Wegg, makes this absolutely explicit.
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness (there are no words to satisfy me) of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
That parenthetical — 'there are no words to satisfy me' — is doing real work.
It tells you that Harmon's gratitude outstrips the language available to him.
In a novel obsessed with valuation — market value, inheritance law, human worth — that failure of language is meaningful.
And to understand the depth of that gratitude, you have to go back to what the Boffins actually risked for young John.
Boffin describes standing up to Old Harmon time after time — and the old man's response was not argument but violence.
There is a passage that is simultaneously appalling and — I confess — very nearly comic in its specificity.

"I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet (she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head), and send it spinning across the yard."
And then — that devastating coda: 'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
The repetition of those two words — Dickens has timed it like a bell.
The black straw bonnet is a masterstroke of novelistic economy.
That parenthetical — 'she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head' — tells you everything about Mrs Boffin's character in twelve words.
She is practical, good-humoured, unpretentious — and therefore, when she is struck down, the outrage is complete.
Dickens has built sympathy through a hat. That is the gift.
This scene matters for another reason: it establishes the Boffins as moral creditors long before they become financial ones.
They advocated for John Harmon when advocacy cost them — personally, physically.
And when that same generosity extends to the Harmon name itself, through Mrs Boffin's proposal, it becomes something genuinely moving.
She wants to find an orphan child, give him John's name, provide for him.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
She doesn't know, of course, that John Harmon is alive and in her house.
The dramatic irony there is almost unbearable.
And that irony is sustained through the entire middle stretch of the novel.
Rokesmith — Harmon — watches the Boffins shower affection on a name that is his own.
He is, in effect, a ghost attending his own wake — and finding it warmer than anything his father ever gave him.
That observation is well put, and it connects to what makes the disguise more than a thriller device.
The identity question in this novel is finally a moral question: what does a man owe to a name, to a fortune, to the people who loved him before he was worth loving?
Harmon's performance as Rokesmith is, in the deepest sense, a testing of what he actually deserves.
A testing, yes — and one conducted in plain sight, for those willing to look.
Coming up, we'll examine another kind of hidden life in this novel — the rooftop world of Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren, and the quiet sanctuary that Riah offers them above the noise of the city.

segments.title: Vice and Virtue: The Novel's Moral Theatre

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been tracing the river and its dead, but this segment turns to something perhaps even darker: the moral theatre Dickens constructs around virtue, vice, and the corrupting gravity of wealth.

With me still are Sir Edmund Leigh, who I suspect has been quietly marshalling his arguments; Professor James Blackstone, whose institutional eye catches what the rest of us romanticise past; and Oliver Trevelyan, who I know has been itching to get to some of the novel's more extraordinary voices.
Let's begin where the novel itself invites us to — with the strange moral logic of old John Harmon's will.
The Boffins are, in many respects, the moral spine of this novel's first movement.
And Dickens earns that claim not through sentiment, but through this rather extraordinary piece of ratiocination from the narrator.

The narrator tells us that old Harmon — the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail, as Dickens names him with magnificent contempt — had scratched at his own stony heart long enough to recognise virtue when he saw it.
"He had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
Now, the moralist in me finds that quite perfect.
Virtue is precisely that which cannot be purchased — and a man who has spent his life purchasing everything at last stumbles upon something real.
It is the novel at its most Johnsonian — the great truth stated with the simplicity that only comes from understanding it bone-deep.
Edmund is right to focus there, and I don't want to flatten the moral point — but I think we also have to register what kind of institution old Harmon ran.
Dickens calls him a jailer, and he means it literally in everything but the iron bars.
The Boffins were tied to that dust heap by economic dependency as surely as any prisoner is tied by chain.
The narrator is careful to say that even while Harmon raged at them, he knew they would not be bought — but he never stopped trying to define every condition of their lives.
Their virtue survives not because they were sheltered, but because they were tested — daily — and held firm.
What strikes me every time I read that passage aloud is the rhythm of the repetition — 'So, even while... So, even while...'
Dickens is hammering a nail, and he wants you to feel each blow.
The old miser is being prosecuted by the narrator — and convicted — but the verdict is almost reluctant, almost tender.
Even Harmon, in Dickens's moral universe, retains a shred of the capacity for recognition — for seeing goodness, even if he can't embody it.
That's a more complicated moral vision than simply staging a villain.
Now, if we are talking about the moral theatre of vice, we cannot avoid Riderhood.
The passage assigned to me — Riderhood's denunciation of Gaffer Hexam — is a masterclass in the rhetoric of false witness.
Listen to the cadence of the accusation, which Dickens writes with a kind of terrible ceremonial force.
"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body.
The hand of Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the hand that done that deed. His hand and no other."
'His hand and no other' — three words that mimic the closure of legal oath while remaining entirely in the dialect of the gutter.
It is mendacity dressed in the grammar of certainty — which is, of course, vice's favourite costume.
And the legal framing is not incidental — 'let me be took down again,' Riderhood says, demanding the apparatus of official record.
He knows how the machinery of accusation works, and he exploits it with considerable sophistication for a man presented as barely literate.
And then there's the alleged confession — the words Riderhood claims Gaffer spoke to him on the river.
"There was foul play then. I done it for his money. Don't betray me!"
Those are words that conform exactly to what a jury of the time would expect a guilty man to say.
Which should make any careful reader profoundly suspicious of them.
The speech rhythms in that confession are extraordinary — 'I done it for his money' has the flatness of someone who has rehearsed, not remembered.
A man genuinely confessing a murder doesn't give you a tidy three-clause summary.
Dickens is letting Riderhood hang himself — or rather, hang Gaffer — with language that is just a little too convenient.
And yet — and this is where Dickens is devilishly clever — we can't be entirely certain he's lying, either.
The reader is left holding the moral uncertainty along with all the other characters — which is precisely where Dickens wants us.
Moral uncertainty is one thing — but I want to draw the contrast, because the novel earns its vices partly by setting them against moments of genuine, almost unbearable goodness.
Jenny Wren's vision of the children in white is, I think, one of the most quietly devastating passages Dickens ever wrote.
And it works, I would argue, not despite its sentimentality but because Dickens earns it through the specificity of Jenny's suffering.
I've read that passage aloud more times than I can count, and it still catches me.
The key — the thing that stops it tipping into pure sentiment — is Jenny's voice at the centre of it.
She sets up the vision with this extraordinary parenthetical — 'in a tone as though it were ages ago' — which tells you everything about what childhood meant to a child like Jenny.
And then the chant of the children — Dickens gives them a refrain that works like liturgy.
"'Who is this in pain! Who is this in pain!' When I told them who it was, they answered, 'Come and play with us!'"
The question repeated before the answer — that's not decoration, that's grief given a formal shape.
What strikes me is how precisely Dickens specifies the contrast — these children 'were not chilled, anxious, ragged, or beaten; they were never in pain.'
That list is not poetic inflation — those are the actual conditions of child poverty in mid-Victorian London, enumerated with the precision of a Poor Law inspector.
Dickens is not asking us to float free into vision — he is grounding the vision in documentary reality.
Jenny's escape into imagination is only legible — only bearable to read — because the reality she's escaping has been so carefully rendered.
And she ends — this tiny, fierce, broken woman — with the most naked plea in the novel.
"O my blessed children, it's poor me. Have pity on me. Take me up and make me light!"
'Make me light' — in a novel whose moral currency is the weight of money and guilt and the dead dragged from the Thames, that phrase does a great deal of work.
It is the counter-weight, if you will, to Riderhood's accusation — the one spoken in the grammar of the powerless, the other in the grammar of the predator.
Dickens understood that moral theatre requires both — and that the audience must feel the full weight of each.
He is not, as some have charged, a sentimentalist.
He is a moralist who trusts his readers to feel before they think — and then to think harder for having felt.
Vice as predation, virtue as the thing that resists purchase, and suffering transformed — through imagination — into a kind of grace.
Three passages, and between them they map something close to the full moral range of this extraordinary novel.
When we return, we'll be looking at the river itself — not just as setting, but as the novel's great moving force, its judge, and its keeper of secrets.

segments.title: Closing: Redemption and the Cost of Truth

utterances.text: We've spent this episode picking apart the novel's great mechanisms — the dust heaps, the river, the market in human beings.
But in these final chapters, Dickens asks a harder question — not what does money do to people, but can people actually escape what money has made them?
The great revelation at the heart of the novel — John Harmon's confession — is where I'd like to end.
Edmund, you've argued throughout that this novel is finally about character under pressure. Does Harmon's revelation satisfy you?
It does — and rather more than that, it moves me.
What Dickens gives us in Harmon's confession is not a man explaining a plot device. It is a man conducting a moral audit of himself.
He returns the verdict aloud to himself — 'Is that so? That is exactly so' — as though he dare not let himself off on a technicality.
And the terms in which he describes his return to England are extraordinary in their honesty.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That accumulation of participles — shrinking, mistrustful, timid, divided — is the cadence of a man unravelling his own self-deceptions with great difficulty and great courage.
Edmund has put his finger on something I find absolutely compelling about that passage as a performer.
Dickens writes it almost like a man dictating his own deposition — checking each clause against the facts of his conscience.
And then there's the scheme itself — because it is quite a scheme.
He describes how he and Radfoot cooked up a disguise, and the phrasing is wonderfully matter-of-fact about something wonderfully absurd.
'The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
'Throwing ourselves in her neighbourhood' — as though they were a pair of slightly damp parcels that destiny might collect.
And yet underneath the comedy there is something genuinely tender about it — a man desperate to know whether he will be loved for himself.
I want to press on the legal and moral tangle that the deception created — because it was genuinely inextricable, and Dickens understood that with precision.
Once Harmon was declared dead and the Boffins came into possession of the fortune, he faced an impossible fork in the road.
To come forward and claim the inheritance meant buying Bella — marrying her under conditions of compulsion.
To stay dead and renounce the fortune meant punishing her for a mercenary instinct she'd already begun to overcome.
Dickens states this with remarkable economy in the very cadence of the prose.
'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
That antithesis — shame versus meanness — leaves no exit. And Dickens knew perfectly well that in real Victorian inheritance law, it would have left no exit either.
James is right to dwell on that passage. And I think what redeems Harmon — morally, not merely legally — is articulated in the passage that follows.
Dickens takes care to show us that the original deception was not born of malice or calculation, but of a damaged soul trying to do right.
The novel insists — and this is the crucial word — it was 'honestly meant well towards her.'
'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood... he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.'
The wretchedness of the childhood — that is doing enormous work here. Burke would have recognised it: a man shaped by circumstances not of his choosing, yet still choosing to be good.
And what I love — and I think it needs to be said plainly — is that Dickens doesn't let the darkness have the last word in these chapters.
He cuts away to Mr Boffin holding forth on the absurdity of charity patronage — and it is a masterclass in comic deflation.
The speech is a glorious thing. Listen to the sheer momentum of it.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses — what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
'Up to his neck' — that image of bureaucratic drowning is so perfectly chosen. The man is being buried alive in performative generosity.
And then Boffin lands the real charge: 'If it ain't stark staring impudence, what do you call it?' He's entirely right. So is Dickens.
Boffin's outburst is funny — but it is also a perfectly accurate description of how Victorian charitable institutions actually operated.
The subscription lists, the ranks of patron and vice-patron — these were real, and they served the donors' vanity far more reliably than the beneficiaries' needs.
Dickens had attended enough charity dinners to know exactly what he was satirising. The target is philanthropy as status performance.
And in this context — placed right beside Harmon's genuine self-examination — the contrast is devastating.
One man tears himself apart to act honestly. A whole class of men rename themselves 'Patron' and call it virtue.
That juxtaposition — Harmon's private moral reckoning against the public theatre of charity — feels like the novel in miniature.
The question the novel keeps asking is who truly earns what they receive — in money, in love, in moral standing.
And Our Mutual Friend's answer, reached through so much mud and river and disguise and grief, is that the earning matters enormously — and is usually invisible to everyone but the earner.
My deepest thanks to Edmund Leigh, James Blackstone, and Oliver Trevelyan for a conversation that has done full justice to a very great novel.
Our Mutual Friend Unpacked. We'll be back.

Then, the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides
      of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and
      under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over
      the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded
      in the rush of smoke and steam and glare. A little more, and again it
      roared across the river, a great rocket: spurning the watery turnings and
      doublings with ineffable contempt, and going straight to its end, as
      Father Time goes to his. To whom it is no matter what living waters run
      high or low, reflect the heavenly lights and darknesses, produce their
      little growth of weeds and flowers, turn here, turn there, are noisy or
      still, are troubled or at rest, for their course has one sure termination,
      though their sources and devices are many.

c8:p43.text:
‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’
c8:p43.summary: Boffin recounts the last time he and Mrs Boffin saw young John Harmon, a seven-year-old being sent to a foreign school, including the poignant moment when Mrs Boffin wept while warming the boy by the fire and embraced him protectively, expressing a desire to save him—a memory that haunted her for years.

      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?

On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

Now, too, was he cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more
      wearisome than remorse. He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold
      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.

      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.

      of number, till he has called us every name he could lay his tongue to. I
      have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the
      claims of the nat’ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin’s bonnet (she wore,
      in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top
      of her head), and send it spinning across the yard. I have indeed. And
      once, when he did this in a manner that amounted to personal, I should
      have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn’t thrown herself
      betwixt us, and received flush on the temple. Which dropped her, Mr
      Lightwood. Dropped her.’

Mrs Boffin pulled his nearest ear, in acknowledgment of this piece of
      philosophy, and then said, gradually toning down to a motherly strain:
      ‘Last, and not least, I have taken a fancy. You remember dear little John
      Harmon, before he went to school? Over yonder across the yard, at our

Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of

c9:p30.text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.
c9:p30.summary: Dickens explains that old John Harmon, despite his misanthropy and greed, respected the Boffins' moral integrity so deeply that he named them in his will as trustees of his fortune.

c12:p93.text:
‘Now let me be took down again,’ said Riderhood, when he had turned the
      drowned cap over and under, and had brushed it the wrong way (if it had a
      right way) with his sleeve. ‘I give information that the man that done the
      Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body. The hand of
      Jesse Hexam, commonly called Gaffer on the river and along shore, is the
      hand that done that deed. His hand and no other.’

‘’Scuse  me , Lawyer Lightwood, it’s a part of the truth, and as such I do
      mind it, and I must mind it and I will mind it. “Rogue Riderhood,” he
      says, “words passed betwixt us on the river tonight.” Which they had; ask
      his daughter! “I threatened you,” he says, “to chop you over the fingers
      with my boat’s stretcher, or take a aim at your brains with my boathook. I
      did so on accounts of your looking too hard at what I had in tow, as if
      you was suspicious, and on accounts of your holding on to the gunwale of
      my boat.” I says to him, “Gaffer, I know it.” He says to me, “Rogue
      Riderhood, you are a man in a dozen”—I think he said in a score, but
      of that I am not positive, so take the lowest figure, for precious be the
      obligations of a Alfred David. “And,” he says, “when your fellow-men is
      up, be it their lives or be it their watches, sharp is ever the word with
      you. Had you suspicions?” I says, “Gaffer, I had; and what’s more, I
      have.” He falls a shaking, and he says, “Of what?” I says, “Of foul play.”
       He falls a shaking worse, and he says, “There  was  foul play then. I done
      it for his money. Don’t betray me!” Those were the words as ever he used.’
